title: Al-Nawawi's forty
hookLine: a Syrian scholar gathers the hadith on which the religion turns
tomorrow: the first hadith on his list is about something nobody can see. what?
last: KEEP ASKING · THEY WERE CAREFUL · UNTITLED TEACHERS

lines: ONE SMALL BAG FOR A HUGE LIBRARY.
cards: One carry-on bag for a long trip. Everything else stays home. Packing like that is mostly saying no: the third pair of shoes, the book you won't finish.
What's left is what the whole trip rests on. Yesterday ended on a question: why would one scholar pick a short list for the whole faith? Because a short list is how you carry something that big.
A scholar from Syria, al-Nawawi, sat down with the huge library of reports about the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and packed one small bag.

teach.b: The word is arba'in, Arabic for forty. In his introduction, al-Nawawi says scholars before him had gathered forties of their own, each on one theme or another.
He wanted something else: hadith that are each a foundation, reports scholars had called the axis the religion turns on, or half of it, or a third.
So the list isn't one topic. It's a set of load-bearing walls in a house: pull one out, and a lot of rooms come down with it. Each day of this block opens one wall and looks at what it holds up.
One thing to tell a friend tonight: count them, and the forty comes to forty-two. The name stayed; the bag got two more things. And he's honest about why he gathered them at all.
A well-known report promises a reward for whoever preserves forty hadith, and al-Nawawi admits the scholars agree its chains are weak.

teach.h: PASS IT TO THE ONE WHO IS ABSENT.
teach.b: So he leans on a sound one instead, from the Prophet's farewell: let the one who is present pass it on to the one who is absent. That's the whole idea of a forty. Small enough to carry, solid enough to pass on.

how: Al-Nawawi's Forty is studied in mosques, schools and homes; students often memorize it in Arabic and read it with a commentary, and copies are easy to find in bookstores, libraries and free editions online.

o: forty: a short hadith collection made to be learned
the forty scholars who first wrote down the hadith
a forty-day fast kept before a holy month begins

games.q: the forty, and the week — tap the pairs.
p: pass it on to the one who is absent

s: al-Nawawi's forty contains exactly forty hadith
count them: forty-two. the name stayed.
al-Nawawi admits the well-known forty-hadith reward report is weak
he says the scholars agree its chains are weak, and leans on a sound report about passing it on.
his forty was the first collection of forty hadith ever made
he says scholars before him had gathered forties of their own. his chose foundations.

games.q: your study group has one hour before an exam that covers a whole semester. one friend wants to skim everything once. what would al-Nawawi's bag suggest?
o: pick the few ideas everything else rests on, and know those well.
skim every chapter once, so nothing is left out entirely.
drill the hardest details, since easy ones take care of themselves.
games.why: faced with a huge library, al-Nawawi didn't skim it. he packed foundations: reports the religion turns on, small enough to carry and pass on.

practice: Take a scrap of paper and write by hand the three things you'd pack if a younger cousin could carry only three from everything this path has given you.
Short lines, no explaining, nothing clever: just what you'd want them to still have years from now. Then rest your hand on the list for the sit and read it once more, slowly.

wordCard.voice: Arba'in. Forty, in Arabic, and the name of a whole kind of book: a short collection made to be learned and passed on. Al-Nawawi's is the one this block opens, one hadith at a time.

orig.note: Arabic: forty. al-arba'in al-nawawiyyah, al-Nawawi's forty, is the collection's usual name.

carryVoice: To pack for today: forty-two foundations, small enough to carry and meant to be passed on. A full week, done.
